item.text: I’ll read the four map parts in order, place all seven notes, write the JSONL update, and run the required check.

item.aggregated_output:
<<12:43 update 2, part 0 of 0..3>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
12:43/q01 Who is the king, and what position does he hold? [ٱلْمَلِكُ · referent] (turns on: The sources give differing personal names or a proposed historical dynasty; none supplies a decisive test.)
  12:43/q01/p1 He is al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, the Egyptian king. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq says he recognized a true vision without understanding it; al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, al-Qurtubi, and Abu Hayyan name him. Al-Alusi calls him an unbeliever; al-Biqa'i describes his political and administrative power.
  12:43/q01/p2 He is al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, Egypt's ruler, with al-Aziz as minister. — reasons: Al-Mawardi gives the name; al-Tabrisi adds the minister.
  12:43/q01/p3 He is probably one of the Hyksos rulers of Egypt. — reasons: Asad proposes Arab origin and kinship with Hebrews to explain his confidence in Joseph and Israelite settlement. Kuranyolu places six Hyksos rulers around 1700–1580 BCE, entering by Sinai; the 'shepherd kings' label suggests Syrian Arabs. It suggests shared nomadic origins with Hebrews and contrasts Moses' later Coptic Pharaoh, citing 2:49.
  12:43/q01/p4 He is the chief king of Egypt. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi gives the political designation without a personal name.
12:43/q02 May an unbelieving ruler be called a king? [ٱلْمَلِكُ · law] (turns on: Whether a royal title implies rightful authority.)
  12:43/q02/p1 Yes, the verse itself calls the unbelieving Rayyan king. — reasons: Al-Alusi cites this title as evidence of permissibility.
  12:43/q02/p2 Some prohibit king or amir when the title implies rightful authority. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports their concern and Muhammad's letter calling Heraclius the 'great Roman.'
12:43/q03 What circumstances led to the king's dream and Joseph's release? [ٱلْمَلِكُ أَرَىٰ · reports] (turns on: The reports differ on whether Gabriel's prior announcement is included and what preceding events are named.)
  12:43/q03/p1 The king's dream arose as Joseph's release approached and became its means. — reasons: Mujahid says the released prisoner's forgotten promise delayed Joseph's release because Satan caused him to forget remembrance of his Lord. Al-Kalbi places seven prison years after five earlier years. Al-Mawardi says the dream also warned of drought for preparation. Al-Biqa'i says God provided another cause for Joseph's elevation after the forgotten request. Islahi links the earlier inmates' dreams and Joseph's interpretations to the king's consultation; God's plan brings unlikely means into being.
  12:43/q03/p2 Gabriel announced Joseph's coming release, power, and reunion before the king dreamed that night. — reasons: Wahb reports the appointed prison term ending. Al-Qurtubi reports Gabriel saying the dream would bring freedom and power.
12:43/q04 Does 'I see' describe a dream or a waking sight? [أَرَىٰ رُءْيَٰىَ · interpretation]
  12:43/q04/p1 It describes a dream seen in sleep. — reasons: Al-Farra says Arabic normally uses this wording for a dream and cites Abraham's explicit sleep vision in 37:102; al-Tabari notes the verse does not itself say 'asleep.' Al-Tabrisi reports this as the majority view. The king later calls it his ru'ya, as Abu Hayyan observes; Study Quran describes it as veridical.
12:43/q05 Why does the king use the present tense 'I see'? [أَرَىٰ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether present tense merely enlivens a past report or hints that the vision recurred.)
  12:43/q05/p1 He vividly recounts a past dream as though seeing it now. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya says he contemplates the vision now; Abu Hayyan calls the scene present to the hearer; al-Biqa'i ties vividness to his alarm. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Alusi explicitly read it as 'I saw.'
  12:43/q05/p2 The wording may indicate a repeated dream. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i compares the earlier prisoners' dreams.
12:43/q06 What did the king see, and how did the images unfold? [سَبْعَ بَقَرَٰتٍۢ سِمَانٍۢ يَأْكُلُهُنَّ سَبْعٌ عِجَافٌۭ وَسَبْعَ سُنۢبُلَٰتٍ خُضْرٍۢ وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتٍۢ · reports]
  12:43/q06/p1 Seven lean cows consumed seven fat cows, and dry ears overcame green ears. — reasons: Al-Suddi says God showed a frightening vision; several accounts say fat cows emerged from a dry river before the lean cows swallowed them, sometimes without visible change, and report the green ears being overcome or consumed. Ibn Atiyya reports the lean cows emerged after the fat and disappeared inside their bellies. Al-Wahidi says none of the fat remained visible; ripe green ears were overcome. The reports vary in these details.
12:43/q07 What do the cows and ears in the dream signify? [سَبْعَ بَقَرَٰتٍۢ سِمَانٍۢ يَأْكُلُهُنَّ سَبْعٌ عِجَافٌۭ وَسَبْعَ سُنۢبُلَٰتٍ خُضْرٍۢ وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتٍۢ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the images principally forecast years, prescribe famine management, or take meaning from contextual dream details.)
  12:43/q07/p1 They forecast fertile years followed by barren years and abundant harvests followed by drought. — reasons: Qatadah assigns fat and lean cows to fertile and barren years and green and dry ears to abundant harvests and drought. Ali says this is the meaning of fat and lean cattle seen in a town. Al-Mawardi calls the dream a warning enabling preparation; Joseph explains it in 12:47–49, as Study Quran notes.
  12:43/q07/p2 The dream chiefly depicts the practical measures needed to survive famine. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i makes fat cows provisions from repeated planting, lean cows shortage, their eating consumption of reserves, green ears stored grain, and dry ears preservation unthreshed. He says unnumbered dry ears fit duties rather than counted famine years.
  12:43/q07/p3 Cattle symbols vary with the dream's setting and details. — reasons: Ali says coastal sailing season can make cows arriving ships; otherwise they may be successive turmoil. Uniform yellow can suggest disease; varied colors, ugly horns, or fiery mouths can signal army, raid, or enemy. Al-Qurtubi adds wife, servant, crop yield, or year because cattle bear offspring and produce yield.
12:43/q08 What does 'fat' mean, and what forms does the word have? [سِمَانٍۢ · meaning]
  12:43/q08/p1 The cows are full of flesh and fat; siman is the plural of samin or samina. — reasons: Al-Nasafi calls it a regular plural; al-Samin notes samina and shared-gender samin like kiram. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin describe saman as noun or verbal noun from samina and samin as active adjective, with irregular vowel pairing; al-Alusi derives forms from samana and samn.
12:43/q09 What does 'fat' grammatically describe, and why? [سَبْعَ بَقَرَٰتٍۢ سِمَانٍۢ · grammar] (turns on: The scope of the adjective: the counted cows or the numeral, with a difference in emphasis.)
  12:43/q09/p1 It qualifies the cows, selecting seven of the fat kind. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf contrasts describing the numeral, which first identifies the count by cow-kind. Abu Hayyan cites the difference between 'three noble men' constructions; al-Samin says an adjective of the genitive classifier makes the counted set possess the quality. Al-Alusi prefers this to describing number and says a derived adjective cannot formally discriminate the count; al-Qurtubi observes another construction is possible outside Qur'anic wording. Al-Zarkashi cites 'seven fat cows' as an example of the rule for agreement of an adjective following the counted expression.
  12:43/q09/p2 Outside this wording, 'fat' can qualify the numeral itself. — reasons: Al-Qurtubi cites a comparable construction at 67:3; al-Tibi says describing the number before its discriminator stresses both count and quality, whereas naming the discriminator first focuses the description.
12:43/q10 Why is the lean cows' number followed directly by an adjective? [سَبْعٌ عِجَافٌۭ · grammar] (turns on: Whether an adjective may itself supply the numeral's counted kind or an understood 'cows' is needed.)
  12:43/q10/p1 The noun 'cows' is understood from the earlier phrase, and lean qualifies the seven. — reasons: Abu Hayyan says the earlier seven cows supply the omitted noun; numerals do not normally take mere adjectives as their genitive discriminator except poetic necessity or substantivized adjectives such as knights. Al-Kashshaf and al-Samin likewise distinguish substantivized nouns; al-Qutb says the prior cows identify the kind. Al-Baydawi ties the feminine form to the understood cows.
  12:43/q10/p2 The adjective may stand for cows as the numeral's discriminator, avoiding an omitted noun. — reasons: Al-Fara'id objects that numerical discriminators normally take genitive construction and offers this alternative; al-Qutb replies that when lean is so used it ceases to be an adjective in the relevant analysis.
12:43/q11 Why is the cows' eating expressed in the imperfect? [يَأْكُلُهُنَّ · rhetoric]
  12:43/q11/p1 It makes a past, startling scene present to the listener. — reasons: Al-Alusi says 'they eat' means 'they ate'; he parses the clause as circumstantial or adjectival.
12:43/q12 What does 'lean' mean? [عِجَافٌۭ · meaning]
  12:43/q12/p1 The cows are extremely emaciated, stripped of flesh and fat. — reasons: Al-Layth defines ajaf as loss of fat; Ibn Durayd describes thick bones bare of flesh. Ibn Atiyya and al-Samin cite a poem about famished Meccans. Al-Raghib relates the root to a thin blade, aversion from food or a person, and thin livestock.
12:43/q13 How is the form 'ijaf' derived and pluralized? [عِجَافٌۭ · grammar]
  12:43/q13/p1 It is an unusual plural of feminine ajfa', patterned after its opposite siman. — reasons: Al-Wahidi, al-Layth, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Alusi, and al-Tabataba'i give analogy with siman; expected alternatives are 'ujuf or 'ujf. Ibn al-Sikkit from al-Farra reports a kasra variant in the root and parallels. Al-Qurtubi gives two verb patterns, 'ajafa ya'jafu and 'ajifa ya'jafu. Al-Tabrisi supplies masculine a'jaf and feminine ajfa'.
12:43/q14 Why are the fat cows mentioned before the lean cows? [سِمَانٍۢ يَأْكُلُهُنَّ سَبْعٌ عِجَافٌۭ · rhetoric]
  12:43/q14/
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<12:43 update 2, part 1 of 0..3>>
p1 They appeared first in the dream. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports seven fat cows emerging from a dry river, followed by seven lean cows that swallowed them without visibly changing.
12:43/q15 What is a sunbula, and what were the green and dry ears like? [سُنۢبُلَٰتٍ خُضْرٍۢ وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتٍۢ · meaning]
  12:43/q15/p1 The green ears bore grain; the dry ears were ripe, curled, and no longer green. — reasons: Al-Baydawi says the green ears had formed grain and the dry ones ripened; al-Alusi adds a report of curling. Al-Biqa'i calls sunbula a reed-like plant with an ordered grain cluster.
12:43/q16 How is 'seven ears' read? [سَبْعَ سُنۢبُلَٰتٍ · readings]
  12:43/q16/p1 Ja'far ibn Muhammad reads sab' sanabil. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi reports this in place of the verse's sunbulat.
12:43/q17 Why use this form and number of ears? [سَبْعَ سُنۢبُلَٰتٍ · rhetoric] (turns on: The notes offer distinct links to 2:261: numerical correspondence or a contrast in crop abundance.)
  12:43/q17/p1 The seven ears correspond to the seven cows and recall the seven-ear parable. — reasons: Ibn Ashur cites 2:261.
  12:43/q17/p2 The numeral modifies a plural of paucity because the dream signifies famine. — reasons: Al-Biqa'i contrasts the multiplied crop in 2:261.
  12:43/q17/p3 The paucity plural sunbulat suits a counted seven or a dream without abundance; the same number takes the abundance plural sanabil elsewhere. — reasons: Al-Zarkashi contrasts sunbulat here with sanabil in another seven-ear verse. Al-Samarra'i says paucity plurals normally denote few, as in contrasting plural pairs, and seven is a small counted set; he says this dream does not call for abundance and notes other plural pairs can distinguish meanings, such as eyes for sight and springs of water.
12:43/q18 Did the dry ears also number seven? [وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتٍۢ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the vision's dry ears represent a counted period or unnumbered duties.)
  12:43/q18/p1 Yes, seven is omitted but supplied by the repeated pattern and 'others'. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi point to the recurring sevens; Abu Hayyan invokes the matching fat/lean and green/dry divisions; al-Biqa'i says the lean cattle have already suggested the count. Al-Tabari glosses 'others' as seven other ears. Al-Alusi says the earlier cows supply it.
  12:43/q18/p2 The dry ears are deliberately unnumbered because the vision describes famine duties, not counted famine years. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i says a forecast reading would require their number.
12:43/q19 How does 'other dry ears' attach grammatically? [وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتٍۢ · grammar] (turns on: The coordinate's scope and whether an omitted numeral or noun is supplied without making the seven green ears also a different dry set.)
  12:43/q19/p1 It coordinates with 'seven', with an omitted seven and understood ears. — reasons: Al-Samin says the matching cow and ear groups supply the numeral; al-Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan, and al-Alusi reject treating 'others' as a modifier of the seven green ears, which would make the same seven both green and other. Al-Samin contrasts 'seven green and dry ears' and al-Kashshaf's standing/sitting men analogy. Al-Alusi prefers ellipsis or Ibn al-Hajib's withdrawal analysis, and argues 'others' is useful emphasis.
  12:43/q19/p2 It coordinates with 'green', leaving the noun 'ears' expressed for both colors. — reasons: Al-Fara'id argues coordination normally repeats the numeral, creating fourteen ears, while an ellipsis analysis might wrongly total seven; attaching at 'green' avoids supplying a new ears noun. Al-Alusi replies that neither repetition nor omission cures the contradiction once a seven-ear discriminator is fixed.
12:43/q20 Is the dry ears' overcoming of the green ears omitted in the wording? [وَأُخَرَ يَابِسَٰتٍۢ · rhetoric]
  12:43/q20/p1 Yes; the cow imagery supplies the action, later clarified by verse 48. — reasons: Al-Baydawi says the ears' state is omitted because cows already explain it; Islahi supplies 'the dry ears consume the green ears' from 12:48.
12:43/q21 Who are the addressed mala'? [ٱلْمَلَأُ · referent] (turns on: Whether the address identifies the court's rank or its interpretive professions; several sources include both.)
  12:43/q21/p1 They are the prominent courtiers or advisers, including leading scholars and sages. — reasons: Al-Tabari calls them nobles and associates; al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi people consulted and followed; al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, and Elmali describe scholars and sages; Abu Hayyan the king's attending officials; Ibn Ashur distinguished people, citing 7:60. Study Quran says high-ranking entourage. Al-Biqa'i says the elite include diviners; al-Tabrisi and al-Alusi report a gathered specialist group.
  12:43/q21/p2 They are magicians, soothsayers, and other dream or omen specialists. — reasons: Al-Suddi lists sorcerers, soothsayers, physiognomists, and bird augurs; al-Qurtubi adds diviners and astrologers. Al-Tabrisi reports this as an alternative to 'elite'; Ibn Ashur cites the Torah's Pharaoh summoning magicians and sages, and observes Egyptian priestly dream interpretation.
12:43/q22 Why did the king seek an interpretation from his council? [يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمَلَأُ أَفْتُونِى فِى رُءْيَٰىَ · interpretation]
  12:43/q22/p1 He found the vision troubling or significant and did not know its meaning. — reasons: Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim say he recognized it as true; al-Mawardi says he announced it broadly so a knowledgeable hearer might explain. Al-Biqa'i says the address signals seriousness rather than a test. Islahi says he suspected his naive courtiers could not interpret it; Elmali says he wanted his difficulty resolved. Al-Alusi reports that calling it a fatwa honors the companions and magnifies the vision. Bint al-Shati says the king twice calls his vision ru'ya because it was clear to him, although his courtiers later call it confused dreams (12:44).
12:43/q23 What does 'give me a fatwa about my vision' mean? [أَفْتُونِى فِى رُءْيَٰىَ · meaning]
  12:43/q23/p1 Explain or interpret the dream and its outcome for me. — reasons: Al-Tabari and Ibn Ashur gloss ifta' as explanation; al-Qurtubi calls it a ruling or interpretation. Al-Tabataba'i reports al-Majma's distinction that a fatwa properly answers a ruling, though the word can answer the matter itself. Al-Wahidi refers to the earlier discussion in al-Nisa'; Ibn Ashur refers to the prison scene at 12:41.
12:43/q24 How does 'fi' connect the fatwa to the dream? [فِى رُءْيَٰىَ · grammar]
  12:43/q24/p1 It figuratively makes the explanation concern and attach to the dream. — reasons: Ibn Ashur compares an explanation attached to a concise matter.
12:43/q25 How is the hamza of 'aftuni' read? [أَفْتُونِى · readings]
  12:43/q25/p1 Readers vary the two hamzas, and some pronounce an intervening alif as waw. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya reports the variants without assigning individual readers. Ibn al-Jazari classifies the adjacent hamzas in al-mala'u aftuni as a damma followed by a fath, among eleven agreed Qur'anic sites of that pairing; 27:32 is another.
12:43/q26 How is 'my vision' or 'the vision' read? [رُءْيَٰىَ لِلرُّءْيَا · readings] (turns on: The variants concern hamza, imala, and final ya pronunciation; the notes assign no semantic difference.)
  12:43/q26/p1 The word has hamza elision and assimilation variants without change of meaning. — reasons: Qiraat-ER gives ruyaaya by hamza elision, pause with silent final ya, and ruyyaya by waw-to-ya assimilation; al-ru'ya likewise has hamzless and assimilated ruyya. Abu Ja'far's assimilated reading is reported by Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, and al-Alusi; grammarians call its phonological sequence irregular because the waw substitution is optional.
  12:43/q26/p2 Ru'ya admits full opening or imala. — reasons: Ibn Khalawayh says imala signals the feminine final alif corresponding to ta'; al-Kisa'i reportedly uses imala here but opening at ru'yaka in 12:5. He says this is mistaken as a case distinction, valid as dialect variation.
  12:43/q26/p3 The first-person ya of 'my vision' is vocalized in one canonical form. — reasons: Qiraat-ER contrasts it with its silence in the standard reading. Abu Amr reports that the Medinans, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr open the first-person ya in the two dream forms, among seven listed forms.
12:43/q27 What kinds of dreams can be true or interpretable? [رُءْيَٰىَ · theology] (turns on: Whether ordinary bodily and mental causes exhaust dreams, or some dreams truly disclose hidden or future realities.)
  12:43/q27/p1 Some dreams disclose real events and can be interpreted, while others arise from the sleeper or deception. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi distinguishes dreams from God or angels, Satanic dreams without interpretation, and dreams from beliefs and prior thoughts. Study Quran calls this vision veridical. Al-Tabataba'i says bodily state, temperament, emotion, chance, and preoccupation shape ordinary dreams; sound dreams disclose future or hidden facts. He argues common experience and noncoincidental fulfillment establish these, while naturalist accounts explain only some dreams. Bint al-Shati distinguishes singular ru'ya, used seven times for a true, clear vision, from plural ahlam, used three times for confused, mixed dreams; she says the king's fulfilled vision is twice called ru'ya here despite the courtiers' description in 12:44.
  12:43/q27/p2 All dreams lack real or scientific connection to external events. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i attributes this to European natural scientists and rejects the universal claim: bodily and emotional causes do not account for sound dreams. He notes some psychologists study dreams.
12:43/q28 How can a true dream disclose hidden realities, and when does it need interpretation? [رُءْيَٰىَ · theology]
  12:43/q28/p1 The sleeping soul connects with higher causes; images may directly show truth or symbolize it. — reasons: Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes physical changing matter, an imaginal realm of immaterial fo

rms causing physical events, and an intellectual realm of universal causes. A strong soul can see universal causes directly; otherwise it clothes them in familiar images. Clear dreams need no interpretation, symbolic images or opposites such as crown/honor and darkness/ignorance do, and tangled transformations resist interpretation.
12:43/q29 What does it mean to 'cross' or interpret a dream? [تَعْبُرُونَ · meaning]
  12:43/q29/p1 It is to pass from dream images to their eventual meaning or outcome. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj, al-Azhari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan, al-Nasafi, al-Alusi, al-Tabataba'i, and Study Quran derive the sense from crossing a river to the far bank; al-Azhari says the interpreter examines both sides and traces beginning to end. Al-Baydawi calls it passage to corresponding psychic meaning, al-Alusi external or inward reality; ta'wil names the destination. Al-Samin cites al-Kashshaf's gloss. The author of al-Nazm compares adjectival usage in 4:90 and 3:7, and replacement of verb by adjective in 7:193.
12:43/q30 Which verb form for interpreting dreams is established? [تَعْبُرُونَ · meaning] (turns on: Established linguistic usage versus the Bedouin poetic attestation of the doubled form.)
  12:43/q30/p1 The light, ungeminated 'abara is the established and stronger usage. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi say authorities reject the doubled verb, ta'bir, and mu'abbir; al-Samin transmits al-Kashshaf, and Ibn Ashur cites his preference. Al-Alusi agrees on the lighter form's strength but acknowledges evidence for the doubled form.
  12:43/q30/p2 The doubled form is attested, although some reject it. — reasons: Al-Mubarrad cites a Bedouin line using dream-interpreter wording; Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Alusi, and Ibn Ashur transmit it. Al-Alusi says the light form remains more established.
12:43/q31 What work does the lam in 'li-l-ru'ya' do? [لِلرُّءْيَا · grammar] (turns on: Whether lam directly marks an object, strengthens fronting, gives direction, or belongs to a different underlying predication or verb.)
  12:43/q31/p1 It clarifies or specifies the object of interpretation. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj and transmitters gloss 'if you interpret, namely the dream'; al-Samin compares 12:20 and proposes 'I mean the dream.' Al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, and al-Baydawi also permit this analysis. Al-Zarkashi gives haita laka at 12:23 as another example of a clarifying lam, glossing it as 'come or approach so that I may speak to you.'
  12:43/q31/p2 It emphasizes or strengthens a fronted object and weakened delayed verb. — reasons: Ibn al-Anbari calls it emphatic; Ibn Atiyya links it to fronting. Abu Hayyan prefers strengthening when the object precedes, not when it follows. Al-Samin says such additions normally need fronting or a derived governor, noting exceptions or containment with 11:107 and 27:72. Ibn Ashur adds foregrounding the dream and cadence. Al-Zarkashi describes the lam as transitive, strengthening a weak verb whose object precedes it, and also cites 23:60. Al-Suyuti likewise calls it emphatic or strengthening when the governing element is weak or delayed.
  12:43/q31/p3 It means 'toward,' directing interpretation to the dream. — reasons: Ibn al-Anbari offers this as an alternative.
  12:43/q31/p4 It is a lam of attachment linking interpreters to the vision. — reasons: Ahmad ibn Yahya gives the sense 'interpreters of the dream.' Al-Zarkashi reports that Basran grammarians call this the lam of annexation, while Ibn al-Anbari calls it instrumental; he also cites 31:14 and 7:62.
  12:43/q31/p5 It belongs to an understood or included verb meaning undertake the dream's interpretation. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf suggests volunteering for the task; al-Samin says ta'burun contains a verb governing lam; Abu Hayyan reports al-Zamakhshari's understood verb; al-Baydawi allows a lam-taking verb. Al-Alusi reports an eagerness reading.
  12:43/q31/p6 The phrase with lam is the predicate of kana, denoting competence in visions. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Samin report this; ta'burun is another predicate or a circumstantial clause. Al-Alusi finds these alternatives strained.
  12:43/q31/p7 It is an extra lam with no independent meaning. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi reports this as a twelfth use of lam and includes 'you interpret the dream' under it, also mentioning 7:154.
  12:43/q31/p8 It is an instrumental lam. — reasons: Al-Zarkashi reports Ibn al-Anbari's description of this lam as instrumental, alongside the Basran description as a lam of annexation; he mentions 31:14 and 7:62.
12:43/q32 Why is 'for the dream' placed before 'interpret'? [لِلرُّءْيَا تَعْبُرُونَ · rhetoric]
  12:43/q32/p1 It foregrounds the dream and maintains the verse's cadence. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the definite article is generic; grammarians also link the position to the strengthening lam.
12:43/q33 What is the predicate of 'if you are' in this phrase? [إِن كُنتُمْ لِلرُّءْيَا تَعْبُرُونَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether ta'burun alone completes kana or the prepositional phrase predicates interpretive competence.)
  12:43/q33/p1 Ta'burun is the straightforward predicate of kuntum. — reasons: Abu Hayyan prefers the apparent syntax over al-Zamakhshari's more complex parses.
  12:43/q33/p2 Li-l-ru'ya is the predicate, with ta'burun a second predicate or circumstance. — reasons: Al-Zamakhshari's analysis is reported by al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, and al-Samin; it conveys competence in dreams. Al-Alusi considers the analysis strained.
12:43/q34 Why did the court fail to interpret the king's dream? [أَفْتُونِى فِى رُءْيَٰىَ إِن كُنتُمْ لِلرُّءْيَا تَعْبُرُونَ · links]
  12:43/q34/p1 They called it confused dreams and said it exceeded their interpretive skill. — reasons: Al-Suddi and Ibn Abi Hatim describe consulted specialists. Al-Razi says they did not deny dream interpretation itself and implied a more skilled interpreter might succeed. Al-Qurtubi and al-Durr report the dismissal. Al-Razi likens a confused dream to a bundle of unrelated plants; al-Harawi derives adghath from bundled grass. Ata and Ibn Abbas call such dreams false, Mujahid a jumble or frightening terrors, Abu Ubayda uninterpretable. Al-Tabataba'i distinguishes tangled transformations from clearer symbolic dreams. Bint al-Shati notes that the Qur'an uses plural ahlam for mixed-up dreams and that the courtiers called this king's clear ru'ya confused dreams at 12:44.
